links.targetTitle: Each SkyLink bridge can be frozen independently from either

title: Freezer thresholds are low enough that most single signing organizations can freeze a bridge alone
content:
Reading the signer allocations against the thresholds produces a result the text never states. The Ethereum multisig is 2/5 with "two (2) addresses controlled by the Core Facilitator and three (3) addresses controlled by Core GovOps" (A.4.2.2.1.2, A.4.2.2.1.3) — so Core GovOps alone clears the threshold, and so does the Core Facilitator alone. Solana is 2/4 split evenly between Soter Labs and Endgame Edge, so **either** organization alone can freeze. Plasma is 2/5 with three Soter Labs seats, so Soter Labs alone can freeze. Avalanche is 2/5 with 2 Soter / 2 Endgame Edge / 1 Grove: two of the three parties can act unilaterally, and Grove cannot act without a partner.

The careful per-organization allocations therefore do not function as a collusion requirement for freezing. They function as a *redundancy* requirement: they guarantee that at least two independent organizations are each individually capable of hitting the stop button, so no single organization's unavailability or refusal can prevent an emergency halt.

This is coherent given the fail-safe reasoning behind the low threshold, but it is easy to misread. A reader who sees "two signers controlled by X, three by Y" naturally infers a checks-and-balances design in which parties must agree. For freeze authority, they need not.

The practical implication is that the real control on abuse is not cryptographic but procedural — the Usage Standards test plus Core Council review after the fact. Anyone assessing SkyLink's trust assumptions should count organizations that can unilaterally halt the bridge (several) rather than reading the seat split as a quorum of peers.
description: Core GovOps holds 3 of 5 Ethereum seats and Soter Labs 3 of 5 Plasma seats against a 2-signature threshold, so the mandated multi-party split does not make a freeze collusion-dependent.
